verses.text: Tethys bore Ocean the swirling Rivers:
Nile, Alpheus, and Eridanus with his deep whirlpools;
Strymon, Maeander, and Ister with his lovely streams;
Phasis, Rhesus, and Achelous with his silver swirls;
Nessus, Rhodius, Haliacmon, and Heptaporus;
Grenicus, Aesepus, and sacred Simois;
Peneus, Hermus, and Caicus with his fine-flowing waters;
great Sangarius, Ladon, and Parthenius;
Evenus, Ardescus, and sacred Scamander.
Tethys also bore a sacred family of daughters, who across the earth
nurture boys to manhood, together with Lord Apollo
and the Rivers. This is the task Zeus has given them:
Peitho, Admete, Ianthe, Electra,
Doris, Prymno, and godlike Urania;
Hippo, Clymene, Rhodea, Callirhoe;
Zeuxo, Clytie, Idyia, Pasithoe;
Plexaura, Galaxaura, and lovely Dione;
Melobosis, Phoe, and beautiful Polydora;
Cerceis, lovely in form, and wide-eyed Pluto;
Perseis, Ianeira, Acaste, Xanthe;
lovely Petraea, Menestho, Europa;
Metis, Eurynome, and Telesto in her saffron-colored robe;
Chryseis, Asia, and enchanting Calypso;
Eudora, Tyche, Amphiro, Ocyroe;
and Styx, the foremost of them all.
These daughters were born to Ocean and Tethys,
the eldest of their daughters, but there are many others.
For there are three thousand slender-ankled daughters of Ocean,
scattered far and wide, watching over the earth and the waters' depths
everywhere alike, glorious children of goddesses.
And there are just as many Rivers, flowing with a roar,
sons of Ocean, whom noble Tethys bore.
It would be hard for a mortal to tell all their names,
but those who live beside each river know its name.
Theia bore great Helios, the Sun, and bright Selene, the Moon,
and Eos, the Dawn, who shines for everyone on earth
and for the immortal gods who dwell in the wide sky,
having yielded to Hyperion in love.
Eurybia, shining among goddesses, joined Crius in love and bore him
great Astraeus, Pallas,
and Perses, whose knowledge set him apart from all others.
Eos bore Astraeus the fierce-hearted Winds:
Zephyrus, who clears the sky, and swift-moving Boreas,
and Notus, after lying with him in love, goddess with god.
After the Winds, Eos, born at daybreak, bore Eosphorus, the Morning Star,
and the gleaming stars that crown the sky.

uncertainties: 354: The supplied Greek reads Φόη, rendered here as Phoe; the earlier draft has Thoe. This may reflect a textual variant or a typo in the Greek.
